title: Plotting to understand, not to present

claims.text: Matejka and Fitzmaurice presented a method for generating datasets that are identical over a number of statistical properties yet produce dissimilar graphs, at the 2017 conference on human factors in computing systems, pages 1290 to 1294. New datasets are generated iteratively from a seed dataset by random perturbation of individual data points, directed toward a desired outcome by a simulated annealing strategy, and the method is agnostic to which statistical properties are held constant. The dinosaur-shaped seed came from Alberto Cairo.

source.title: Justin Matejka and George Fitzmaurice, Same Stats, Different Graphs: Generating Datasets with Varied Appearance and Identical Statistics through Simulated Annealing, Proceedings of the 2017 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, pages 1290 to 1294, doi 10.1145/3025453.3025912

claims.text: Cleveland and McGill identified a set of elementary perceptual tasks that people carry out when extracting quantitative information from graphs, and formulated a theory ranking them by the accuracy of the resulting judgements. From most to least accurate the ranking runs: position along a common scale; position along non-aligned scales; length, direction and angle; area; volume and curvature; then shading and colour saturation. The ordering was derived from ten common graph types, with formal experiments using about 50 subjects.
tokens: Journal of the American Statistical Association

source.title: William S. Cleveland and Robert McGill, Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application to the Development of Graphical Methods, Journal of the American Statistical Association 79(387):531-554, 1984

claims.text: The same authors cautioned against what they called the conceptual trap of adopting accuracy as the sole criterion for judging a graphical form, and their design principle is stated comparatively: a form whose perceptual tasks lead to more accurate judgements than another form conveying the same information will increase the chances of correct perception of patterns and behaviour.

source.title: William S. Cleveland and Robert McGill, Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application to the Development of Graphical Methods, Journal of the American Statistical Association 79(387):531-554, 1984

beats.broke: one word covers two different jobs — finding out what is in the data, and convincing somebody of a conclusion — and the standards that make a plot good at one make it bad at the other
beats.fix: separate them deliberately: disposable, ugly, numerous plots for yourself while you are still finding out, and one carefully encoded plot for the reader once you know what the claim is
beats.cost: the second job requires choosing an encoding, and encodings are not a matter of taste — they have a measured ranking by accuracy, which is itself not the only criterion that matters
